paras: The disfranchisement of Black voters in the Richmond district in 1880 was the exclusion, on election day, November 2, 1880, of voters in Virginia's Third Congressional District who had paid their poll tax to collectors appointed by the Readjuster State Auditor. Election judges rejected the receipts under an injunction issued the night before by Judge William Izard Clopton of Manchester, and a letter to the New-York Tribune alleged that men at the Richmond polls threatened Black voters with 'mob law' and tore up their receipts. Three Manchester election judges were indicted in federal court for refusing the votes of Black men.

Virginia law required a voter to have paid a $1 poll tax before election day, and according to the Tribune letter, Black men who applied at the Hustings Court clerk's office were misdirected and delayed. Auditor John E. Massey then appointed special collectors, among them William H. Beveridge in Richmond, and the same letter said Beveridge's office was attacked on the Sunday night before the election and his signs torn down. On the night of November 1, regular Democrats obtained from Judge Clopton an injunction restraining election judges from recognizing the collectors' receipts, served, John S. Wise later wrote, 'at sundown, the day before election'.

By 12:50 p.m. on election day, Republican observers F. C. Loveland and F. A. Burr telegraphed that judges had already thrown out 400 to 600 receipts. The Tribune's unsigned Richmond correspondent wrote that 'exconvicts, blacklegs, Ku-Klimx and others' stationed at the polls threatened Black voters with the penitentiary and 'mob law', tore up their receipts, and handed them to police, who held them until sundown. No other report found describes threats or torn receipts at the Richmond polls.

Across the river at Third Ward, Manchester, a Conservative challenger, C. L. Page, came to the polls determined to challenge holders of the receipts, and two Democratic judges refused 13 or 14 Black men, among them Richard Crump, who said he was handed back his receipt and told to 'stand aside'. George D. Wise, the regular Democrat, was returned the winner over John S. Wise by 2,365 votes.

In a card published November 27, John S. Wise estimated that he lost about 1,300 votes to the injunction and to Funder judges who followed it, but he called the Richmond count 'the fairest count ever made in this city' and declined to contest the seat. Early in December the Manchester judges R. B. Foster, James Galloway and Samuel Logan, the last a Black Republican, were arrested, and U.S. Commissioner Atkins found the rejected receipts valid and held them in $500 bail. A federal grand jury indicted the three on December 9 after Judge Hughes advised that the receipts had been legally issued, and their trial opened before him on February 18, 1881. The trial jury failed to agree and was discharged, and no further proceedings appear in the coverage found.

Republican papers carried the election-day telegram under headings such as 'Alleged Sharp Practice in Richmond' and among 'reports of intimidation in the South', and the New-York Tribune printed the Richmond letter under 'Democratic Methods in Virginia'. The Readjuster Valley Virginian argued that 'the negro' was 'the primary object of assault' of the poll-tax restriction, while the Democratic Richmond Dispatch ridiculed Loveland and Burr as 'Radical emissaries' and called their telegram a 'libel upon Judge Clopton'.
The Richmond Dispatch reported the federal hearings at length, naming the rejected voters, while brief wire reports of the arrests, bail and indictment ran in New York, Washington and Knoxville.

Witnesses at the federal hearing disagreed over Logan: the clerk and the two Democratic judges said all three concurred, while the supervisor, two Black witnesses and Logan himself said he argued that the men should vote and gave way to Foster. The election-day telegram attributed the injunction to a Richmond 'corporation judge' named Ould, whereas the later Richmond reports and Wise named Clopton of Manchester.

reader.title: Disfranchisement of Black voters in the Richmond district, 1880
bases: The only account of threats against Black voters at the Richmond polls is a letter alleging men 'threatened the negroes with the penitentiary and with mob law' and tore up their receipts (A9); every other report describes exclusion of voters by injunction and election judges, with no physical attack on any voter (A2, A11, A14).

The exclusion of Black voters holding the Auditor's collectors' receipts is corroborated by many independent reports (A1, A2, A8, A11, A14, A18), but the threats of mob law, torn receipts, police detentions and the attack on Beveridge's office appear only in one unsigned letter (A9).

accounts.label: Republican observers' telegram
accounts.gist: On election day judges were throwing out all receipts from the Auditor's collectors under an injunction, 400 to 600 by midday, a 'last desperate attempt of the Bourbons'.

accounts.label: Anonymous Richmond letter
accounts.gist: Black taxpayers were obstructed by the court clerk, Beveridge's office was attacked, and at the polls stationed men threatened Black voters with the penitentiary and 'mob law', tore up receipts and had them held by police until too late to vote.

accounts.label: Defeated candidate John S. Wise
accounts.gist: About 1,300 legal voters were excluded by Clopton's injunction and Funder judges, but the Richmond count was fair and he could not prove wider intimidation, so he would not contest.

accounts.label: Federal hearing testimony
accounts.gist: At Manchester's Third Ward a challenger and two Democratic judges refused 13 or 14 Black men with Auditor's receipts; witnesses disagreed on whether the Black judge Logan concurred.

accounts.label: Democratic press
accounts.gist: The Richmond Dispatch dismissed the Republican telegram as a libel on Judge Clopton.

framing.detail: Republican papers ran the telegram as 'Alleged Sharp Practice' and among 'reports of intimidation in the South', and the Tribune headlined the letter 'Democratic Methods in Virginia'.
The Readjuster Valley Virginian said the poll-tax restriction's 'primary object of assault' was 'the negro'.
The Democratic Richmond Dispatch mocked the 'Radical emissaries' and defended Judge Clopton.
Wire reports of the arrest, bail and indictment ran without comment across the country.

versions.value: Black voters were threatened with 'mob law', their receipts torn up and they were held by police until sundown
Voters were excluded by judges' rejection of receipts; the Richmond count was 'the fairest'; no proof of wider deterrence
